summary: The note describes the Mark 10 torpedo, put into use by the United States in 1915 and derived from the Mark 9 aircraft torpedo converted for submarine use. It was the primary torpedo of the R- and S-class submarines, used alcohol-water steam turbine propulsion, and had the largest warhead of any U.S. torpedo developed at that time. It was succeeded by the problematic Mark 14 but stayed in service through the Pacific War, and Mark 10 Mod 3 stockpiles were used extensively early in World War II.
one_line: The Mark 10 torpedo, a 1915 U.S. submarine torpedo derived from the Mark 9 aircraft torpedo, used through much of the Pacific War.
key_facts: The Mark 10 torpedo was put into use by the United States in 1915.
The Mark 10 was derived from the Mark 9 aircraft torpedo converted to submarine use.
The Mark 10 was used as the primary torpedo in the R- and S-class submarines.
The Mark 10 used alcohol-water steam turbine propulsion.
The Mark 10 was succeeded by the problematic Mark 14 torpedo.
The Mark 10 remained in service in S-boats and fleet submarines through the Pacific War.
The Mark 10 featured the largest warhead of any U.S. torpedo developed at that time.
Stockpiles of Mark 10 Mod 3 torpedoes were used extensively during the first part of World War II.
Mark 10 Mod 3 torpedoes were used because of short supply of the newer and longer Mark 14 torpedoes.
Some fleet submarines carried a mixture of Mark 10 and Mark 14 torpedoes on patrol.
